issue_context.title: `systemd-networkd` automatically adds interface route for DNS while DNS is in separate subnet while there is classless static route available to the DNS subnet
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

253.5

### Used distribution

NixOS 23.05

### Linux kernel version used

6.1.37

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

networkctl

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

No additional interface routes are added.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

In the specific network, I get the following configuration via DHCP:

- my_ip: `172.0.0.244/24`
- gateway: `172.0.0.1`
- dns1: `10.0.0.153`
- dns2: `10.0.0.153`
- classless, static route: `10.0.0.0/8 via 172.0.0.1`

I confirmed that only this one route is advertised in the DHCP response using WireShark.

Despite that, I get two additional routes:

- `10.0.0.153 dev wlp3s0`
- `10.0.0.154 dev wlp3s0`

These route break the setup: because they are interface routes for the specific target netdev, they are preferred over the classless static route advertised by the DHCP server. Any try to contact the DNS fails, because `wlp3s0` only has a `172.0.0.x/24`, which has no direct way of reaching `10.x.x.x/8`. If I remove the two additional routes manually, my device uses the advertised gateway to reach `10.x.x.x` and everything works.

The respective `.network` file is really boring:

```ini
[Match]
Name=wl* ww*

[Network]
DHCP=yes
LLMNR=false
MulticastDNS=resolve

DNSSEC=no
```

### Steps to reproduce the problem

_No response_

comments:
Setting

```
[DHCPv4]
RoutesToDNS=false
```

Circumvents the problem. I still believe this is likely a bug, why would the default configuration (`RoutesToDNS=true`) configure an obviously nonsensical route? The route is obviously nonsensical, because:

- DHCP advertises a route that makes the DNS's network reachable
- The added routes can't work, because they demand an interface to send data directly to a network despite that interface not heaving any IP in said network

> If not found, skip to configure the route.

"skip to" is used with a target. E.g. "skip to the end". If you want to skip *over* something, you don't use "to". E.g. "skip over the middle", "skip the middle".

"If not found, do not configure the route." or "If not found, skip configuration of the route.".
